content: When preterm birth is considered imminent, antenatal corticosteroids should be administered if there is no clinical evidence of maternal infection, adequate childbirth care is available (including the ability to recognize and manage preterm labor and birth safely), and the preterm newborn can receive appropriate care if needed (such as resuscitation, thermal care, feeding support, infection treatment, and safe oxygen use). This recommendation is strongly supported by moderate-quality evidence for newborn outcomes and low-quality evidence for maternal outcomes. Antenatal corticosteroids are recommended for women at risk of preterm birth, regardless of whether a single or multiple birth is anticipated. This recommendation is based on low-quality evidence. For women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes and no clinical signs of infection, antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended. This is supported by moderate-quality evidence for newborn outcomes and low-quality evidence for maternal outcomes. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is not recommended for women with chorioamnionitis who are likely to deliver preterm. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. For women undergoing planned cesarean section at late preterm gestations (34–36+6 weeks), antenatal corticosteroid therapy is not recommended. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended for women with hypertensive disorders in pregnancy who are at risk of imminent preterm birth. This recommendation is strongly supported by moderate-quality evidence for newborn outcomes and low-quality evidence for maternal outcomes. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended for women at risk of imminent preterm birth of a growth-restricted fetus. This recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence. For women with pre-gestational and gestational diabetes at risk of imminent preterm birth, antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended, accompanied by interventions to optimize maternal blood glucose control. This recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence. Intramuscular dexamethasone or betamethasone (total 24 mg in divided doses) is recommended as the antenatal corticosteroid of choice when preterm birth is imminent. This recommendation is based on low-quality evidence. A single repeat course of antenatal corticosteroids is recommended if preterm birth does not occur within 7 days after the initial dose, and subsequent clinical assessment indicates a high risk of preterm birth in the next 7 days. This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence for newborn outcomes and low-quality evidence for maternal outcomes. Tocolytic treatments (both acute and maintenance) are not recommended for women at risk of imminent preterm birth to improve newborn outcomes. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Magnesium sulfate is recommended for women at risk of imminent preterm birth before 32 weeks of gestation to prevent cerebral palsy in the infant and child. This recommendation is strongly supported by moderate-quality evidence. Routine antibiotic administration is not recommended for women in preterm labor with intact amniotic membranes and no clinical signs of infection. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence. Antibiotic administration is recommended for women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes. Erythromycin is the antibiotic of choice for prophylaxis in these cases. However, the use of a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid (co-amoxiclav) is not recommended. These recommendations are based on moderate-quality evidence. Routine delivery by cesarean section to improve preterm newborn outcomes is not recommended, regardless of cephalic or breech presentation. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Routine perineal or pubic shaving before vaginal birth is not recommended. Routine vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine during labor to prevent infectious morbidities is also not recommended, even in women with group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonization. However, intrapartum antibiotic administration is recommended for women with GBS colonization to prevent early neonatal GBS infection. These recommendations are based on varying levels of evidence. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for women undergoing operative vaginal birth or episiotomy. However, it is recommended for women undergoing manual removal of the placenta or those with thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears. These recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence. For women undergoing cesarean section, prophylactic antibiotics should be administered before skin incision rather than intraoperatively after umbilical cord clamping. A single dose of first-generation cephalosporin or penicillin is preferred for prophylaxis. Vaginal cleansing with povidone-iodine immediately before cesarean section is also recommended. These recommendations are based on varying levels of evidence. Induction of labor is recommended for women who have reached 41 weeks of gestation. However, it is not recommended for women with uncomplicated pregnancies at less than 41 weeks or for suspected fetal macrosomia at term. For women with prelabor rupture of membranes at term, induction of labor is strongly recommended. These recommendations are based on varying levels of evidence. Oral misoprostol (25 µg every 2 hours) and low-dose vaginal misoprostol (25 µg every 6 hours) are recommended for induction of labor. However, misoprostol is not recommended for induction in women with a previous cesarean section. Low doses of vaginal prostaglandins and the use of a balloon catheter are also recommended for induction. These recommendations are based on moderate-quality evidence. For women with uterine hyperstimulation during labor induction, betamimetics are recommended. However, outpatient induction of labor is not recommended for improving birth outcomes. These recommendations are based on low-quality evidence. Active phase partograph with a four-hour action line is recommended for monitoring labor progress. Digital vaginal examinations every four hours are recommended for routine assessment and identification of delays in active labor. These recommendations are based on varying levels of evidence. The use of oxytocin alone is recommended for treating delays in labor. However, high starting and increment dosages of oxytocin, oral misoprostol, or amniotomy alone are not recommended for labor augmentation. These recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence. For the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), the use of uterotonics during the third stage of labor is recommended for all births. Oxytocin (10 IU, IV/IM) is the preferred uterotonic drug. In settings where oxytocin is unavailable, other injectable uterotonics or oral misoprostol (600 µg) are recommended. These recommendations are based on moderate-quality evidence. Late cord clamping (performed 1–3 minutes after birth) is recommended for all births while initiating essential newborn care. Early cord clamping (<1 minute after birth) is not recommended unless the neonate requires immediate resuscitation. These recommendations are based on moderate-quality evidence. Postpartum women should receive regular assessments of vaginal bleeding, uterine contraction, fundal height, temperature, and heart rate during the first 24 hours after birth. Urine voiding should be documented within six hours. These recommendations are based on existing WHO guidelines. At each postnatal contact, women should be assessed for general well-being, including urinary and bowel function, perineal wound healing, pain, breastfeeding progress, and emotional well-being. Women should also be observed for signs of domestic abuse and provided with information on whom to contact for advice and management. These recommendations are based on existing WHO guidelines. Women should be counseled on the physiological recovery process after birth, signs of complications (e.g., PPH, pre-eclampsia), nutrition, hygiene, birth spacing, and family planning. Contraceptive options should be discussed, and methods provided if requested. Women in malaria-endemic areas should use insecticide-treated bed nets. Early mobilization and gentle exercise are encouraged during the postnatal period. These recommendations are based on existing WHO guidelines. Psychosocial support by a trained person is recommended for preventing postpartum depression in high-risk women. However, routine formal debriefing or distribution of printed educational materials for this purpose is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. These recommendations are based on low-quality evidence. Women who have lost their baby should receive additional supportive care. Health professionals should provide opportunities for women to discuss their birth experience during their hospital stay. These recommendations are based on existing WHO guidelines.
